articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities in Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Actions
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations on November 13, 2026, targeting entities involved in counter narcotics and counter terrorism activities.

These actions aim to disrupt financial networks and operations supporting illicit drug trafficking and terrorist organizations, reinforcing the U.S. commitment to combating these threats globally. The specific entities and individuals targeted were not immediately detailed in the initial announcement but are expected to be listed on the SDN List.

articles.headline: OFAC Updates Iran-Related SDN Listing for Volta Shipping Services
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) updated its Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List on November 9, 2026, regarding an Iran-related entity.

The update specifically changed the listed alias for Volta Shipping Services LLC, a UAE-based company linked to Mohammad Hossein Shamkhani, from Volta Shipping Services FZCO to Volta Container Line FZCO. The company remains designated under Executive Order 13902 and continues to be subject to secondary sanctions risk.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / ABA Banking Journal

articles.headline: OFAC Sanctions Eight Canada-Based Money Services Businesses Tied to Iran's Digital Asset Sector
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) designated eight Canada-based money services businesses on November 6, 2026, for their alleged involvement in Iran's digital asset sector.

These businesses are accused of facilitating transactions involving Iran, including converting Iranian currency into digital assets and conducting transactions with sanctioned Iranian exchanges and digital asset addresses linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). This action, part of 'Operation Economic Outcast,' was coordinated with FinCEN and Canada's FINTRAC under Executive Order 13902, targeting international financial channels used by Iran to evade sanctions.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / ABA Banking Journal / Steptoe

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Cyber-Related and Transnational Criminal Organizations; Expands Cuba Sanctions to Four Key Sectors
body: On November 5, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting cyber-related and transnational criminal organizations, alongside significant new sanctions against Cuba.

OFAC sanctioned four individuals and 41 entities linked to the Cambodia-based Prince Group transnational criminal organization (TCO), and separately designated Malaysian national Chui Kok Wa, identified as the leader of a Madagascar-based scam network targeting U.S. citizens. Concurrently, OFAC issued a determination extending Executive Order 14404 to four additional sectors of the Cuban economy: manufacturing, technology, electronics, and marine, paving the way for further sanctions on entities operating within these areas.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / Reuters / Herbert Smith Freehills

articles.headline: OFAC Sanctions Fraudulent Ship Registries Supporting Iran's Shadow Fleet; Amends Venezuela-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on November 4, 2026, targeting an India-based network providing fraudulent maritime flagging and registration services to Iran's 'shadow fleet.'

This network, allegedly led by Suniel Kumar Sharma and Jaspreet Preeti Shahid, provided false flags and certifications to sanctioned vessels transporting Iranian petroleum, including those operating on behalf of Iran's military and its proxies. Concurrently, OFAC issued an alert warning against the Iranian shadow fleet's reliance on false flags for sanctions evasion. In a separate action, OFAC issued an amended Venezuela-related General License (GL 5AA), authorizing transactions related to the Petróleos de Venezuela, S.A. 2020 8.5 percent bond, effective December 18, 2026, replacing GL 5Z.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an amended Iran-related General License on October 29, 2026.

This amendment provides updated guidance or authorizations for certain transactions involving Iran, though the specific details of the changes were not immediately released. General Licenses typically aim to clarify or expand permissible activities under existing sanctions regimes.

articles.region: North Korea, Democratic Republic of the Congo
articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities in North Korea and Democratic Republic of the Congo
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations on October 28, 2026, targeting entities in North Korea and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

These actions are part of ongoing efforts to counter illicit activities and human rights abuses in these regions. The designations aim to disrupt financial networks and support structures for the targeted regimes and individuals. This follows a joint statement by the EU, Australia, and the US on October 28, reaffirming their commitment to target DPRK's use of overseas workers, malicious cyber activities, and unlawful DPRK-Russia cooperation.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends FAQs on Blocking and Rejecting Transactions and Filing Reports
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued amended Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) on October 26, 2026.

These amendments provide updated guidance regarding the blocking and rejecting of transactions, as well as the procedures for filing reports with OFAC. The updates are intended to clarify compliance obligations for financial institutions and other entities subject to OFAC regulations.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Iran-Related Designations, Removes Belarus and North Korea Listings, and Issues New General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on October 21, 2026, while also removing certain entities from its Belarus and North Korea sanctions lists.

In addition, OFAC issued new Iran-related and Russia-related General Licenses and amended Frequently Asked Questions. These actions reflect a dynamic approach to sanctions, adjusting measures based on ongoing geopolitical developments and compliance needs.

articles.headline: EU Imposes New Sanctions on 113 Russian Individuals and Entities, Targeting Financial, Energy, and 'Shadow Fleet' Sectors
body: The Council of the European Union approved new restrictive measures on November 16, 2026, adding 12 individuals and 101 entities to its sanctions lists targeting Russia.

These sanctions aim to further restrict Russia's ability to finance its war against Ukraine, specifically targeting key sectors of the Russian economy, including nearly 50 Russian banks and financial institutions, oil refining businesses, and support networks for Russia's 'shadow fleet.' The measures also include individuals and entities involved in supplying the Russian military and financing the war, as well as those responsible for Russia's hybrid activities against third countries and international organizations.

Among the newly listed entities are several Russian financial institutions, major Russian oil refineries, and companies in the United Arab Emirates, China, Seychelles, and Oman that purchase Russian crude oil or petroleum products. The sanctions entail asset freezes and travel bans for listed individuals, and prohibit EU citizens and companies from making funds or economic resources available to them.
articles.source: Council of the European Union / European Pravda / CEO Magazine Poland

articles.headline: UK Designates Oil Tanker 'APEKS' for Involvement in Russian Oil Transport
body: The UK government, through the Office of Financial Sanctions Implementation (OFSI), announced new sanctions on November 12, 2026, designating the oil tanker IMO 9274616, also known as 'APEKS'.

The designation is based on reasonable grounds to suspect that 'APEKS' is involved in activities that destabilize Ukraine or undermine its territorial integrity, sovereignty, or independence, specifically by transporting Russian oil or oil products from Russia to a third country.

The sanctions impose prohibitions on providing technical assistance, crew services, operating services, chartering services, brokering services, financial services, or funds to the specified ship. Additionally, services related to the acquisition, sale, transfer, or supply of 'APEKS' are prohibited.

articles.headline: EU Imposes Anti-Dumping Duties on Cold-Rolled Flat Steel Products from Five Countries
body: The European Commission announced on November 16, 2026, the imposition of anti-dumping duties on imports of certain cold-rolled flat steel products from India, Japan, Taiwan, Türkiye, and Vietnam.

The decision follows an investigation that found these products were being imported into the EU at dumped prices, harming the European industry. The definitive anti-dumping duties range from 3% to 27.9%, depending on the country of origin.

The Commission stated that these measures are designed to effectively protect the EU industry from unfair trade practices, particularly in light of Chinese overcapacity impacting global steel markets.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.
